extracted.intended_audience: Federal agency NEPA practitioners, agency counsel, Tribes, and other NEPA stakeholders/commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining the significance of environmental effects (context and intensity factors) under NEPA and for establishing and using categorical exclusions (CEs) consistent with CEQ's final rule. Intended to guide agency environmental review, EIS determinations, and CE substantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of intensity (degree) of effects in determining significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze the intensity of effects (the 'degree' of the action's effects) as part of the significance determination, using the list of intensity factors as applicable to the proposed action and in relation to one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ reinstated 'intensity' as a consideration; intensity factors have long provided guidance on how the intensity of an action's effects may inform significance. CEQ does not consider 'intense' synonymous with 'significant'—intensity factors inform the assessment. The term 'effect' is defined to mean reasonably foreseeable effects, so the intensity analysis applies to reasonably foreseeable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only adverse effects can be significant
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant effects are adverse effects; CEQ retains 'adverse' in the regulatory text and interprets 'significant effects' to be those that are damaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ limits 'significant effects' to adverse effects via the definition in §1508.1(mm). Agencies still must identify and discuss all reasonably foreseeable effects (beneficial and adverse) in an EIS, but only adverse effects can be 'significant.' This interpretation is supported by NEPA's policies and recent statutory amendments referencing 'negative environmental impacts' and 'significance of adverse effects.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonably foreseeable effects (implicit in 'effect' definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses and intensity-factor considerations apply only to reasonably foreseeable effects because 'effect' is a defined term meaning reasonably foreseeable effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ declined to repeatedly insert 'reasonably foreseeable' in the intensity factors because the definition of 'effect' already bounds the analysis to reasonably foreseeable effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider duration of effects and evaluate on an effect-by-effect basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider the duration (short-term and long-term) of effects and evaluate duration within each individual effect category rather than weighing across categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ revised §1501.3(d) to encourage agencies to consider duration 'in assessing context and intensity' and made 'effects' singular to emphasize effect-by-effect analysis. Agencies may consider that an effect could be adverse in the short term and beneficial in the long term, but must evaluate significance for each effect category and time period; some short-term harms may be significant regardless of later benefits (illustrative habitat restoration and groundwater recharge examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on netting across effect categories (no offsetting adverse effects with beneficial effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies may not offset an action's adverse effects by counting benefits in other effect categories (no 'netting' across environmental effects) to avoid preparing an EIS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added text prohibiting agencies from offsetting adverse effects with beneficial effects to determine significance and provided a parenthetical example (may not offset adverse effect on one species with beneficial effect on another). The regulations have never allowed net benefit analysis across effects to inform NEPA review level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on public health and safety (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider 'the degree to which the proposed action may adversely affect public health and safety' when assessing intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ revised the factor to focus on public health and safety and declined suggestions to add broader or less precise terms such as 'welfare' or 'public well‑being' because 'public health and safety' has a more precise meaning and longstanding practice since 1978.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on unique characteristics of the geographic area (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the degree to which the action may adversely affect unique characteristics such as historic or cultural resources, parks, Tribal sacred sites, prime farmlands, wetlands, wild and scenic rivers, or ecologically critical areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ reinstated and modernized the 1978 factor (changed 'park lands' to 'parks') and declined to broaden 'prime farmlands' to all farmland. The list is illustrative and not exhaustive; agencies can consider other factors appropriate to the action. Other intensity factors may capture related Tribal/Indigenous concerns (e.g., historic resources, resources listed or eligible for the National Register).

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the action may violate relevant laws or policies (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the action may violate relevant Federal, State, Tribal, or local laws or other requirements, or be inconsistent with policies designed for protection of the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ revised wording to 'actions that may violate relevant Federal, State, Tribal, or local laws' and added 'other requirements' and 'inconsistencies' with environmental protection policies. CEQ declined to list specific laws in the regulation as unnecessarily specific, but agencies may do so in their NEPA procedures. Weight given to statutes vs. policies may differ, and agencies should consider coordination (e.g., with coastal programs) where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which effects are highly uncertain (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the degree to which the effects of the action are highly uncertain when assessing intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ restored 'highly uncertain' from the 1978 regulations and declined to use 'highly controversial' to avoid conflating technical uncertainty with public controversy. CEQ also declined to substitute 'high degree of uncertainty' because 'highly uncertain' is longstanding regulatory language and preserves parallelism and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid segmentation; consider cumulative effects as part of 'effects' (related to intensity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must consider the relationship of the action to other actions with adverse effects and avoid segmenting actions to evade significance determinations; cumulative effects are addressed within the definition of 'effects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ proposed a separate factor regarding relation to other actions but ultimately did not restore separate text; instead cumulative effects are included in the definition of 'effects' and the prohibition on segmentation is addressed in §1501.3(b) (scope of an action and effects). Agencies should consider cumulative (direct, indirect, and cumulative) effects and not segment actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on historic resources listed or eligible for the National Register (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the degree to which the action may affect historic resources listed or eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ reinstated this longstanding 1978 factor and declined to expand it to include State or Tribal equivalents to registers; the list of intensity factors is not exhaustive and agencies have experience considering this matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on endangered or threatened species and their habitat (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the degree to which the action may adversely affect an endangered or threatened species or its habitat, including habitat that has not been designated as critical habitat under the ESA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ expanded the 1978 regulatory text to capture habitat impacts regardless of critical habitat designation, aligning NEPA review with ESA section 7 consultation practice. CEQ rejected narrowing to only designated critical habitat because important habitat use may not align with regulatory critical habitat designations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree to which action may adversely affect communities with environmental justice concerns (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the degree to which the action may adversely affect communities with environmental justice concerns, including disproportionate adverse effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added this factor and revised the phrasing to 'adversely affect' for consistency with other factors. The intensity factors inform a determination of significance, and 'effect' is defined to mean reasonably foreseeable effects; CEQ declined to further define 'degree to which' in the rule text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects upon rights of Tribal Nations reserved through treaties, statutes, or Executive orders (intensity factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider effects upon rights of Tribal Nations that have been reserved through treaties, statutes, or Executive orders when determining whether an effect is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ added this factor and sought Tribal input. The factor addresses the unique rights of Tribal Nations in a nation-to-nation relationship; CEQ declined to broaden this factor to include non‑Tribal indigenous rights not denominated as Tribal Nations. CEQ noted related considerations appear elsewhere in the intensity factors (e.g., historic/cultural resources, environmental justice, violations of law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish CEs consistent with §1507.3(c)(8) and ensure appropriate substantiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must establish categorical exclusions (CEs) consistent with §1507.3(c)(8) and may use mechanisms outside of their NEPA procedures to establish CEs, while ensuring CEs are appropriately substantiated and bounded to actions that normally do not have significant effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ intends changes to promote agency use of CEs where appropriate, providing flexibility while requiring proper substantiation and bounds so CEs apply only to actions that normally do not have significant effects. Agencies must identify in their NEPA procedures which CEs require documentation (§1507.3(c)(8)(i)). CEQ declined to require advance public notice or publication of documentation for every CE as overly burdensome, but agencies may choose to notify the public and make documentation available where appropriate given public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: When establishing a CE, consider applicability 'individually or in the aggregate'
rubrics_metrics.description: When substantiating a CE, an agency must determine that the category of actions covered by the CE will not have significant effects 'individually or in the aggregate'—i.e., consider the effects of a single action and the aggregate of multiple actions covered by the CE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CEQ reinstated this phrasing to reflect the statutory concept of a 'category of actions' and to ensure agencies consider both single actions and repeated collective application of a CE over time. 'In the aggregate' was chosen instead of 'cumulatively' to avoid confusion; because 'effects' includes cumulative effects, agencies should consider direct, indirect, and cumulative effects of individual and aggregated actions and bound analyses by reasonable foreseeability. Agencies have flexibility in how to evaluate aggregate actions and may consider extraordinary circumstances to avoid multiple actions covered by the CE having reasonably foreseeable significant aggregate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and public transparency for CEs should be calibrated, not automatic
rubrics_metrics.description: CEQ declines to require agencies to provide public notice in advance of using a CE or to publish documentation of every CE determination; agencies must identify which CEs require documentation and may choose to publicize determinations where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An across-the-board public-notice or publication requirement would burden agency resources and undermine CE efficiency. Agencies can identify processes or specific CEs in their NEPA procedures for which they will make determinations publicly available, and CEQ encourages agencies to notify the public and make documentation available when public interest is expected.
